newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pork sales to Japan may keep hogs above $50.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pork sales to Japan may keep hogs above $50.

text.p: U.S. hog producers can expect cash hog prices to average $50 per hundredweight (cwt) or better for the rest of this year if Japan steps up purchases of U.S. pork, said Glenn Grimes, a University of Missouri agricultural economist.
Without increased Japanese purchases, he said hog prices could average in the mid-$40s the rest of 1997.

"If they (Japan) do hold off until September and purchase heavily in September, October, November and December, we could sustain the market at $50 or better," Grimes said during an interview while attending the World Pork Expo under way here.
Cash hogs in direct Iowa/southern Minnesota trade on Thursday sold at a top price of $59.00 per cwt, the U.S. Agriculture Department reported.

U.S. pork sales to Japan were expected to rise after foot- and-mouth disease was reported in Taiwan hogs in March. At that time, Taiwan banned exports of its pork indefinitely, and several countries including Japan, banned imports of Taiwan pork. Taiwan had been the number one supplier of pork to Japan.
So far, Grimes said, U.S. pork sales to Japan have been disappointing, possibly because Japan may have a lot of pork in storage, which could sustain it until September.
Grimes said with fourth-quarter U.S. pork production expected to be up four to five percent from a year ago, sales to Japan would be needed to keep hog prices above $50.

An outbreak of hog cholera in the Netherlands also could support U.S. hog prices, because Denmark, which currently exports pork to the U.S., would likely divert some of that supply to Europe to offset the loss of Netherlands pork.
Grimes forecast 1998 hog prices to average in the mid-$40s and through the year 2000, hogs may average above $40.

"Right now we don't see prices below $40 through 2000," he said, assuming the U.S. will have nine-billion to 10-billion- bushel corn harvests each year. "For the good producer it will be profitable at that level."

Because of environmental and space concerns, plus a shift toward more-arid climates, Grimes said hog production is gradually moving out of the Midwest and in 10 years "there is some possibility ten percent of the hogs produced will be within 100 miles of Guymon, Okla."
"We are moving the hogs south and west. The current signs point in that direction," he said.
He said other sites for increased hog production could be Colorado and Wyoming.
